title: If Marriages Are Lasting Longer, How Can We Make Them Last for Life?
author: Daisy Mae Inglese
summary: Writing for Restoring the West, Daisy Mae Inglese responds to UK figures showing that marriages ending in divorce now last an average of 13 years, the longest on record. She argues that longevity alone is no cause for celebration, since 42 percent of marriages are still predicted to end in divorce in 2026 and the consequences reach beyond the household into society. She points to the ease of online no-fault divorce, introduced in 2022, and the high cost of couples counselling at about 80 pounds a session as signs that support for struggling couples is thin. Her deeper claim is that marriage has been secularized into a civil contract with a get-out clause, and must be recovered as a religious commitment of sacrificial love. She adds that family breakdown costs the UK economy roughly 47 billion pounds a year and concludes that the West must recommit to marriage as sacred.
points: Longer-lasting marriages that still end in divorce are not progress, so the real question is what would help marriages last for life.
Frictionless online divorce, set against the cost of counselling at around 80 pounds a session, leaves struggling couples with an easy exit and little support.
The author does not argue that every couple must stay together, and she excludes relationships that are dangerous or harmful.
She traces many endings to a secularized view of marriage as a civil contract, and calls for recovering marriage as a religious pledge of sacrificial love.
Family breakdown has public costs, including an estimated 47 billion pounds a year to the UK economy and greater risks of poverty and harm to children's mental health.
quotes: Marriages may be lasting longer, but longevity alone is no cause for celebration. The end of a marriage is not simply a private affair between two adults. Its consequences reach far beyond the home and into society itself.

Since the introduction of no-fault divorce in the UK in 2022, ending a marriage has become easier than ever. You can initiate a divorce from your iPhone on your commute to work, using the Government’s online platform to initiate the process, without speaking to another person.
The average cost of couples counselling is £80 per session, putting it out of reach for many whose marital difficulties already center on finances.
Supporting marriage does not mean that every couple should stay together. No one should be forced to remain in a relationship that is dangerous or harmful.

Marriage has become increasingly secularized: a civil contract with a get-out clause and, for some, a mere token Instagram display. For marriage to survive every season of life, it must be rooted in something deeper.
We must recover the understanding of marriage as ultimately a religious commitment, one of sacrificial love and a final, heroic surrender of freedom to another.
The question we should be asking is not why marriages are lasting longer, but what would help them last for life.
